clue.text: Endlessly sick, I had cared about sugar

indicators.note: about signals that the gathered letters are moved around into a new order
endlessly tells us to drop the final letter of the word sick

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone feeling permanently ill blames their own past caring about sweet things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' cuts the K from SICK to leave SIC; 'about' rearranges SIC plus IHADCARED.
explanation.definitionFit: A disaccharide is a sugar molecule made of two simple sugars joined, such as sucrose.

clue.text: Hesitant after written account replaces one article with another

indicators.note: replaces tells us one article inside the diary word is swapped for another article

parts.note: a diary is a written account of daily events

explanation.surface: Someone dithers after a diarist changes the articles in their text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replaces one article with another' swaps the indefinite article A in DIARY for the definite article THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Dithery describes someone wavering and unable to decide, which is being hesitant.

clue.text: One collecting hard stones along the shore

indicators.note: collecting means the first word gathers the other letter inside it

parts.note: single means one
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone collects hard pebbles on the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingle is a mass of small rounded pebbles found on beaches.

clue.text: Old king on journey engaging good poet

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed on top of, so the king comes first

parts.note: Old King Cole is the merry old soul of the nursery rhyme

indicators.note: engaging means holding the other letter within, as gears engage

parts.note: a ride is a journey

explanation.surface: An ancient king sets out on a journey taking along a fine poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the nursery-rhyme monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English Romantic poet, author of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

clue.text: Famous cricketer: he passed on tip for boy in high school

indicators.note: in means the following letters are placed within the abbreviation for the school

parts.note: OB, short for Latin obiit, means he died, as on gravestones

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its first letter, here of boy

explanation.surface: A celebrated cricketer passes on advice to a schoolboy.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Hobbs was a great English batsman of the early twentieth century. 'he passed on' looks like giving advice, but it means died: OB.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Jack Hobbs was one of England's most celebrated opening batsmen in cricket history.

clue.text: Regarding place for sporting contests as generator of income

parts.note: RE means regarding or concerning, as in business letters
a venue is a place where games or matches are held

explanation.surface: A stadium is seen as a money-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenue is the money an organisation takes in, its income.

clue.text: Act in which to see pest put down

indicators.note: in which means the first word holds the second inside it

parts.note: a deed is an act
a rat is a common pest

explanation.surface: A deed in which vermin are exterminated.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests putting a pest down, but 'put down' is the definition: lowered in rating.
explanation.definitionFit: Derated means given a lower rating or value, so reduced or brought down in standing.

clue.text: Chief praying effusively and moralising in sermon

indicators.note: effusively means pouring out without restraint, so the letters tumble into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A leading cleric prays gushingly while lecturing the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'effusively' rearranges CHIEF and PRAYING.
explanation.definitionFit: Preachifying means delivering tedious moral lectures, as a sermon might.

clue.text: Court procedure subsequently holding one right back

indicators.note: back means the whole construction is read from end to start
holding means the first word contains the other letters

parts.note: later means subsequently
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A court case is later held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts IR inside LATER to make LAIRTER, which 'back' turns around.
explanation.definitionFit: A retrial is a second hearing of a case in a law court.

clue.text: Old kingdom has sailor returning with very short song

indicators.note: returning means the sailor's letters are read backwards

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor
V is the short form of very
an aria is a song in an opera

explanation.surface: An old realm boasts a sailor coming home with a brief tune.
explanation.walkthrough: AB reversed gives BA.
explanation.definitionFit: Bavaria was a kingdom from 1806 to 1918 and is now a German state.

clue.text: Drunken refrains here? One clears an obnoxious atmosphere

indicators.note: drunken suggests reeling and jumbled, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Drunken singing fills a room that needs something to clean the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunken' rearranges REFRAINS and HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deodorising spray or device masks or removes unpleasant smells in a room.

clue.text: Fury, perhaps, of archdeacon in time meeting resistance

indicators.note: in means the archdeacon's letters go within the word for time

parts.note: an age is a period of time
VEN, the Venerable, is the title of an archdeacon
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: An archdeacon's fury builds over time and meets opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: The Furies of Greek myth were spirits of vengeance, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Furies pursued wrongdoers, so a Fury is an example of one who exacts revenge.

clue.text: Member of parliament is older, one being absent for a time

indicators.note: being absent for means one letter leaves and a time steps in its place

parts.note: senior means older

explanation.surface: An MP is getting on, and missing for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one being absent for a time' removes I (one) from SENIOR and puts A T (a time) in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A senator sits in a senate, the upper house of a legislature.

clue.text: See expression of surprise after sending back games expert

indicators.note: sending back means the pieces together are read in reverse

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city and so a bishop's see
oh is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A games guru exclaims in surprise upon returning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sending back' reverses ELYOH. Edmond Hoyle wrote the standard rules of card games.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmond Hoyle was an 18th-century authority on card games, hence the phrase according to him.

clue.text: Part of a letter from one who has already reached the heights?

definitions.meaning: the tail of a letter like g or p that drops below the line

definitions.text: one who has already reached the heights?
definitions.meaning: a climber who has made it to the top can only come down

explanation.definitionFit: A descender is both the downward stroke of letters like p and someone going downhill after the summit.

clue.text: Cutie nods naughtily in this act maybe

indicators.note: naughtily means misbehaving, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An attractive person nods mischievously, hinting at a flirtatious act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naughtily' rearranges CUTIE and NODS.
explanation.definitionFit: Seduction is the act of enticing someone, which the flirting described could be.

clue.text: Out of jail, one prisoner being embraced and finely bedecked with gold?

indicators.note: being embraced means the letters are held inside the larger word

parts.note: freed means let out of jail
I is the Roman numeral for one
lag, as in old lag, is slang for a prisoner

explanation.surface: A released convict hugs a fellow inmate, dripping with gold jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: LAG is British slang for a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: Filagreed means decorated with delicate gold or silver wirework, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Half a decade of brilliance cut short with little hesitation

indicators.note: cut short means the final letter is lopped off the word for brilliance

parts.note: lustre means brilliance or sheen
um is a brief hesitant sound

explanation.surface: Five years of splendour end abruptly, after a moment's pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' removes the E from LUSTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lustrum is a period of five years, from the Roman census held every five years.

clue.text: One's icy and more lacking in expression when speaking

indicators.note: when speaking means the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: glassier means more glazed or expressionless, like a glassy stare

explanation.surface: One person is cold and more blank-faced while talking.
explanation.walkthrough: A glassy stare is blank, so GLASSIER, said out loud, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A glacier is a slow-moving mass of ice, so it is something icy.

clue.text: Narratives to be read both ways

indicators.note: read both ways means the answer is the same from either end

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Stories that read the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagas are long heroic tales, originally Norse or Icelandic narratives.

clue.text: Quiet little devils consuming last of our seafood

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet

indicators.note: last of means the final letter of the word our

parts.note: imps are little devils

explanation.surface: Quiet little rascals tuck into the last of our seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consuming' puts R, the last of OUR, inside IMPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrimps are small crustaceans eaten as seafood.

clue.text: One heading off into tedious work grimaced

indicators.note: into means the trimmed word goes within the word for tedious work

parts.note: a grind is tedious, laborious work

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter of one is removed

explanation.surface: Someone forced to set off for dull work pulls a face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One heading off' reads like a person setting out; 'heading off' actually beheads the word, leaving NE for 'into' to place.
explanation.definitionFit: A grin is a facial expression like a grimace, so grinned means pulled a face.

clue.text: Coffee in street obtained by worker

parts.note: an ant is a worker insect

explanation.surface: Coffee bought in the street by a worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Instant is a type of soluble powdered coffee.

clue.text: Note bed cast outside home after complete upset

indicators.note: complete upset means the whole construction is turned upside down in a down clue
cast outside means the first word is thrown round the second

parts.note: a cot is a bed
in means at home

explanation.surface: A note says a bed was thrown out of the house after a total upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like the start of a message but is the definition, the keynote of a scale; 'cast outside' makes CINOT and 'complete upset' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: The tonic is the keynote, the first degree of a musical scale.

clue.text: My pleasant artistic moulding

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like my!
nice means pleasant

explanation.surface: Someone admires a lovely piece of decorative moulding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation here, as in 'My, how nice!': COR is the British equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: A cornice is an ornamental moulding running round the top of a wall or building.

clue.text: Adoring fans of ancient king

indicators.note: fans means spreads out, so the letters of adoring are dispersed into a new order

explanation.surface: Devoted admirers of a king from antiquity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fans' looks like the noun, but it is a verb rearranging ADORING.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordian relates to Gordius, the Phrygian king who tied the famous knot cut by Alexander.

clue.text: One relatively short distance seen absurdly as huge

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
MM, millimetres, is a short unit of distance

indicators.note: absurdly means the letters of seen are put into a ridiculous order

explanation.surface: One short distance appears absurdly vast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absurdly' rearranges SEEN to give ENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Immense means extremely large, enormous.

clue.text: Given a non-U treatment?

parts.note: non-U looks like lower class, but here it means stripped of the letter U, as in US spellings like color

explanation.definitionFit: American spelling drops the U from words like colour and honour, so text so treated is made transatlantic.
